title: Uniphase, a small laser maker, goes public
what: Uniphase, a San Jose company started in a garage in 1979, has listed its shares on the Nasdaq. It makes gas lasers used in instruments for biotechnology, semiconductor manufacturing and printing, and since June sells the Ultrapointe laser system that inspects chips for defects. Sales were about $27 million in the fiscal year to June 1993, with a small loss after patent litigation costs.
why: The listing beat (importance 1). A tiny industrial laser maker that, through acquisitions, became the largest optical component supplier of the telecom boom. The IPO price and exact date were not found; the listing month comes from the Form 8-A filed November 15, 1993 and the game's first price.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/912093/0001012870-96-000044.txt (1996 prospectus with financial history and reference to the 1993 Form 8-A, read 2026-10-03); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/912093/0000891618-96-002144.txt (10-K 1996, read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JDS_Uniphase (read 2026-10-03)

title: Uniphase enters fibre-optic telecommunications
what: Uniphase acquired Uniphase Telecommunications Products, a maker of high-speed modulators and transmitters for long-distance fibre-optic networks and cable television, on May 15. It is Uniphase's first step into telecommunications equipment.
why: The pivot that made the company: within five years fibre-optic parts were nearly all of its business.

title: Uniphase sells shares at $30 and splits
what: Uniphase sold 2 million new shares at $30 each, raising $60 million, and approved a two-for-one share split. In May it bought two British and American fibre-optic packaging companies. Net income for the nine months to March rose to $5.7 million.
why: Growth financed with stock, the pattern of the next four years.

title: Uniphase bets on multi-wavelength fibre
what: In its annual report Uniphase described wavelength division multiplexing, which sends up to 16 signals of light down one fibre and multiplies network capacity, as the market for its modulators and amplifier lasers. Sales in fiscal 1996 had risen 63% to $69.1 million, mostly from the telecom unit bought in 1995.
why: The technology that made the late-1990s boom possible, and Uniphase's position in it.

title: Uniphase to merge with JDS Fitel
what: Uniphase agreed on January 28 to combine with JDS Fitel of Ottawa, a leading maker of passive fibre-optic components, in an exchange of shares. Together they will be one of the largest suppliers of parts for fibre-optic networks, whose traffic is growing fast with the internet.
why: The merger that created JDS Uniphase and launched one of the great runs of the bubble (+1,097% in the twelve months to February 2000).
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/912093/0000912093-99-000065.txt (8-K referring to the merger agreement of January 28, 1999, read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JDS_Uniphase (read 2026-10-03)

title: JDS Uniphase is born and splits its shares
what: Uniphase and JDS Fitel completed their merger on June 30; the company is now called JDS Uniphase. On July 8 the board approved a two-for-one share split. The company is buying competitors at a rapid pace.
why: The first of three two-for-one splits approved between July 1999 and January 2000 (per the 10-Qs; Wikipedia describes the three as 3:1, 2:1 and 2:1).

title: JDS Uniphase's sales quadruple
what: JDS Uniphase's sales in the quarter to September were $230 million, up 301% from a year earlier, helped by the merger and by demand for components used in networks that send many wavelengths of light down one fibre. The board has approved a second two-for-one split.
why: The optical frenzy: +47% in October, +34% in November, +45% in December 1999. The figures are from the quarterly filing (filed November 4); the date of the results release in late October was not confirmed.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/912093/000091209399000097/0000912093-99-000097-d1.html (10-Q for the quarter to September 30, 1999, read 2026-10-03)

title: JDS Uniphase buys Optical Coating Laboratory
what: JDS Uniphase agreed on November 3 to merge with Optical Coating Laboratory (OCLI) of Santa Rosa, California, a maker of optical thin-film coatings, in exchange for shares.
why: The first of three giant stock-financed takeovers (OCLI, E-TEK, SDL) that later had to be written off.

title: JDS Uniphase agrees to buy E-TEK
what: JDS Uniphase agreed on January 17 to merge with E-TEK Dynamics of San Jose, another maker of fibre-optic components, in a share deal valued at about $15 billion. Two weeks earlier the board approved another two-for-one split.
why: The shares peaked a month later (2000-02); the company paid for its purchases with stock valued at bubble prices.

title: JDS Uniphase to buy SDL for about $45 billion in stock
what: On July 9 the boards of JDS Uniphase and SDL, a San Jose maker of pump lasers for fibre-optic amplifiers, approved a merger in which SDL holders receive 3.8 JDS Uniphase shares for each SDL share, a deal valued at about $45 billion. SDL must pay a $1 billion fee if it backs out.
why: One of the largest technology takeovers ever, agreed at the top of the telecom bubble; most of its value was written off a year later.

title: JDS Uniphase closes SDL deal and warns
what: JDS Uniphase completed its merger with SDL on February 13 after selling a Zurich laser plant to Nortel to satisfy the Justice Department. On the same day it warned that customers' visibility is low and that they are reducing inventories, and gave lower guidance. Telecom carriers are cutting their spending.
why: The start of the crash: -51% in February 2001.

title: JDS Uniphase cuts its forecast again
what: On March 6 JDS Uniphase lowered its guidance: sales of about $925 million in the quarter to March and flat or slightly higher sales in the June quarter. It cited uncertainty about carriers' capital spending and customers working down inventories.
why: One warning after another in the spring of 2001; -31% in March.

title: JDS Uniphase writes off about $50 billion
what: JDS Uniphase is writing down the goodwill from its stock-financed acquisitions; the reduction of goodwill and other assets for the fiscal year to June comes to $50.1 billion, the largest write-off by any company so far. It is cutting its workforce from about 29,000 at the start of the year to 13,000 and closing factories to save $700 million a year.
why: The defining event: the bubble's paper wealth erased in one charge. The workforce eventually fell to about 5,300 and the shares from their peak to below $2.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/912093/0000912093-01-500022.txt (8-K with conference call, read 2026-10-03); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/912093/000109581101504970/f75587e10-k.txt (10-K for fiscal 2001, read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JDS_Uniphase (read 2026-10-03)

title: JDS Uniphase keeps cutting
what: JDS Uniphase said its Global Realignment Program has cut annual costs by about $1.1 billion at a cost of about $978 million, and it plans further cuts. It holds $1.36 billion in cash and short-term investments.
why: Survival mode at the bottom of the telecom bust; the shares had fallen below 10 in game terms (-98% from the peak).

title: JDS Uniphase's sales grow again
what: JDS Uniphase reported sales of $153 million for the quarter to December, up 4% from the previous quarter and above its guidance, and a smaller loss before restructuring charges.
why: The first signs of stabilisation; +40% in January 2004, but the shares fell back during the year.

title: JDS Uniphase buys Acterna and moves into test equipment
what: JDS Uniphase completed its purchase of Acterna, a maker of test and measurement equipment for telephone and cable companies, on August 3, for about $450 million in cash and 200 million shares.
why: The beginning of the business that became Viavi: testing networks rather than building them.

title: JDS Uniphase proposes a reverse split
what: On September 23 JDS Uniphase asked shareholders to authorise a reverse share split of between one-for-eight and one-for-ten, to be voted on at the December annual meeting. Its shares trade below $2.
why: A reverse split of one-for-eight followed; game prices are adjusted for it.

title: JDSU's profit at a five-year high
what: On January 31 JDSU reported revenue of $366.3 million for the quarter to December and net income of $23.2 million, its highest in five years, against a loss a year earlier.
why: Test equipment from Acterna gives the company a steadier business; the recovery did not last through 2008.

title: JDS Uniphase wins the Connecticut securities trial
what: A jury acquitted JDS Uniphase and four executives in a lawsuit brought by the state of Connecticut, which claimed they had hidden their knowledge of the coming downturn in 2000-01 from shareholders.
why: A rare securities case that went to trial; it closed the chapter of the bubble years.

title: JDS Uniphase's chief executive steps down
what: JDS Uniphase reported sales of $380.7 million for the quarter to September, up 6.6% from a year earlier, and expects $366 million to $392 million in the December quarter. Chief executive Kevin Kennedy announced he will step down at the end of the year.
why: The financial crisis hits: -36% in October and -50% in November 2008, to the lowest level since 1994.

title: JDS Uniphase's sales drop 27%
what: On April 29 JDS Uniphase reported sales of $280.6 million for the quarter to March, down 27% from a year earlier, and a net loss of $85 million including a $45 million goodwill impairment. It cut inventory and debt and holds $673.5 million in cash.
why: The bottom of the business cycle; the shares nevertheless rose 42% in April with the market rebound (see Unexplained moves).

title: JDS Uniphase's sales jump 39%
what: On February 3 JDS Uniphase reported sales of $477 million (before adjustments) for the quarter to December, up 39% from a year earlier and 16% from the previous quarter, and net income of $23.6 million.
why: The post-crisis recovery in optical networks; +45% in February 2011, the best month since 2002. The gains were lost by the end of the year.

title: JDSU slips back into a loss
what: On May 2 JDSU reported revenue of $409.2 million for the quarter to March, down from $454.0 million a year earlier, and a net loss of $17.4 million.
why: The optical recovery of 2010-11 fades; the shares fell 17% in May 2012.

title: JDSU buys Network Instruments
what: JDSU announced it is acquiring Network Instruments, a network performance management company, for $200 million.
why: Another step towards network testing and monitoring software.

title: JDSU splits in two: Viavi and Lumentum
what: On August 1 JDSU distributed 80.1% of its optical components business, Lumentum, to its shareholders and renamed itself Viavi Solutions. Viavi keeps the network test and measurement business and optical products for anti-counterfeiting and 3D sensing.
why: The end of JDS Uniphase. The game follows Viavi; the price history is adjusted for the spin-off, so the separation itself does not show as a drop (the -15% of August 2015 is the market move).

title: Oleg Khaykin takes over Viavi
what: Viavi named Oleg Khaykin president and chief executive, with interim chief Richard Belluzzo becoming chairman.
why: Khaykin was still running the company in 2026.

title: Viavi beats its guidance
what: Viavi reported revenue of $201.8 million for the quarter to December, down 2.3% from a year earlier but above the top of its guidance. Chief executive Oleg Khaykin pointed to strong demand from telecom service providers.
why: A small, stable company in these years; +12% in February 2018.

title: Viavi's sales up 49%
what: On February 5 Viavi reported sales of $306.9 million for the quarter to December, up 49% from a year earlier, and its strongest financial performance since becoming Viavi, according to chief executive Oleg Khaykin.
why: Viavi's fastest growth in years; +18% in February 2019.

title: Covid-19 hits Viavi's sales
what: Viavi reported sales of $256.2 million for the quarter to March, down 3.4% and below its guidance, and said the Covid-19 pandemic was the main reason, as customers delayed purchases. It gave no forecast for the next quarter.
why: A modest dent; the shares recovered during 2020.

title: Viavi recovers from the pandemic
what: Viavi reported revenue of $303.4 million for the quarter to March, up 18.4% from a year earlier, at the high end of its guidance, as demand for network test equipment recovered.
why: A steady recovery after the pandemic dip.

title: A challenging quarter for Viavi
what: On November 3 Viavi reported sales of $310.2 million for the quarter to September, down 5.1% from a year earlier. Chief executive Oleg Khaykin called it 'a challenging quarter'.
why: Slowing telecom spending; the shares fell 25% in November 2022 and drifted lower into 2024.

title: Viavi loses Spirent to Keysight
what: The board of Spirent, a British telecom testing company, accepted a £1 billion takeover offer from Viavi, but later in the month recommended a higher offer of £1.16 billion from Keysight.
why: A failed attempt at a large acquisition; Viavi later bought parts of Spirent's business from Keysight.

title: Viavi rides data-centre demand
what: On October 16 Viavi completed the purchase of Spirent's high-speed Ethernet, network security and channel emulation testing business from Keysight. On October 29 it reported quarterly sales of $299.1 million, up 25.6%, driven by data-centre and aerospace and defence customers.
why: The AI build-out of data centres reaches the test-equipment makers; +39% in October 2025.

title: Viavi's sales up 36%
what: On January 28 Viavi reported sales of $369.3 million for the quarter to December, up 36.4%, at the high end of its guidance, and expects strong demand from the data-centre ecosystem and defence customers to continue.
why: +37% in January 2026, the start of a run that tripled the shares in four months.

title: Viavi's sales up 43%
what: On April 29 Viavi reported sales of $406.8 million for the quarter to March, up 42.8%, ahead of its expectations, driven by data-centre and aerospace and defence customers, and forecast higher sales for the June quarter.
why: The biggest monthly gain in the whole arc (+57%), in a strong month for the market (+10%); Viavi is now valued as an AI supplier.
